newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Iberian short end to follow forex whims.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Iberian short end to follow forex whims.

text.p: Iberian bonds will keep a sharp lookout for European monetary union jitters next week, analysts said on Friday.
The short end of the yield curve is expected to reflect trends in the foreign exchange markets, recovering only if the peseta and the escudo regain stability.
Long bonds will remain pegged to Italian volatility, while Spanish paper is likely to be penalised by monthly Treasury actions on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"The short end of the yield curve suffered most from the change we had in rate expectations after recent peseta weakness. We had a flattening in the curve, but this part is also set to gain most if calm is restored," said Maria Victoria Nunez, economist at Societe Generale.
At midday on Friday the peseta was trading at around 84.88/90 per mark, slightly stronger than early levels at 84.92, when dealers reported buying intervention by the Bank of Spain.
Dealers think the Bank of Spain will continue to support its currency, especially after Thursday's comment by Bundesbank.
Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said exchange rate criteria for membership in the planned single European currency would play a "decisive role".
"We expect the short end to perform better than recently. But we don't see any rush after such peseta weakness," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
But shorter bills and notes should offer more value in Spain than in Portugal, where inflation is lagging behind and the central bank seems to have less power to defend its currency.
"In Portugal, notes could wait to recover as they are more vulnerable to the forex market as they have less reserves and their central bank could delay a rate cut," said Fernandez.
On the cash market Portuguese three-year bonds were trading at a yield of around 6.0 percent, while their Spanish counterparts were at around 5.80 percent.

"At the moment the short end of the yield curve is paying 20 to 40 basis points more than its Spanish counterpart, due to the fact that our inflation is lagging behind Spain," said Nuno Godinho, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon.
This spread should be reduced to zero as time goes on, with Portuguese CPI expected to fall from April onward, and Spanish inflation seen hitting a low in May, he said.
The Portuguese CPI rose 0.3 percent month-on-month in January to take the year-on-year to 3.3 percent. Spanish CPI rose 0.3 percent in January, up 2.9 percent on the year.
Long term yields offer a different viewpoint, with Spain paying more than Portugal "because of our better economic performance, but also because of a lower degree of liquidity" said Godinho.
On Friday Spanish 10-year cash bonds spread over Bunds was trading at around 132 basis points, with its Portuguese counterpart trading at around 124 basis points.
These two levels hit record lows of between 83 and 80 points when euphoria over the two countries' chances of joining the single currency was at its height at the end of January.

The spread widened after northern political and business leaders expressed doubts that the so-called 'Club Med' countries --Italy, Spain and Portugal-- would or should gain entry to monetary union at the start in January 1999.
The long term spread should remain stuck in a narrow range, following the Italian market, economists said.
"Our market is starting to think that Spain will be let in (to EMU) only when Italy enters, so we'll move together," Fernandez said.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
